items.prompt: What is it called when a solid turns into a liquid?

options.why: Freezing is a liquid turning into a solid.
Evaporating is a liquid turning into a gas.
Condensing is a gas turning into a liquid.

hints: Think about ice on a hot day.
The solid gets warm and becomes runny.
What happens to ice cream in the sun?
items.explanation: Melting is when a solid is heated and turns into a liquid, like ice turning into water.

items.prompt: Match each change to its name.
hints: Two changes need heating and two need cooling.
Freezing happens in a freezer.
Think of a puddle drying up for liquid to gas.
items.explanation: Melting is solid to liquid and freezing is liquid to solid. Evaporating is liquid to gas and condensing is gas to liquid.

items.prompt: The thermometer is in melting ice. What temperature does it show?

figure.alt: A thermometer from minus 10 to 20 °C. The liquid is level with the 0 °C mark.

hints: Find the top of the liquid.
Read the number next to it.
Ice melts at the same temperature that water freezes.
items.explanation: Ice melts at 0 °C, which is also the temperature at which water freezes.

items.prompt: This thermometer is inside a freezer. What temperature does it show?

figure.alt: A thermometer from minus 20 to 20 °C, marked every 5 degrees. The liquid stops at the line for minus 15 °C, below zero.

hints: The liquid is below zero.
Numbers below zero are negative.
Count down in 5s from 0.
items.explanation: The liquid stops three marks below zero, and each mark is 5 degrees. The freezer is at minus 15 °C.

items.prompt: Ice is heated in a pan. Put the changes in order.
items: water boiling and turning into water vapour
hints: Start with the coldest state.
The ice must melt before the water can boil.
Boiling happens at the hottest point.
items.explanation: Heating melts the ice into water. The water gets hotter until it boils at about 100 °C and turns into water vapour.

items.prompt: Wet clothes dry on a washing line. Where does the water go?

options.text: It soaks into the washing line.
options.why: A line is thin. It cannot hold all that water.
The water is not destroyed. It becomes a gas in the air.
Water cannot turn into dust.

options.text: It evaporates into the air as water vapour.

hints: The water leaves the clothes slowly.
Liquid water can change into a gas.
What do we call a liquid turning into a gas?
items.explanation: The water evaporates. It turns into water vapour, an invisible gas that mixes with the air.

items.prompt: Why do clothes dry faster on a hot, windy day?

options.text: Warmth and wind both make water evaporate faster.
Wind blows water back into the clothes.
options.why: Wind carries water vapour away from the clothes.

options.text: Clothes dry at the same speed on any day.
options.why: Weather changes how fast water evaporates.

options.text: Cold air makes water evaporate faster.
options.why: Water evaporates faster when it is warm, not cold.

hints: Drying means the water evaporates.
Think about drying clothes on a cold, still day.
What do heat and wind each do to evaporation?
items.explanation: Warmth gives water the energy to evaporate faster. Wind carries the water vapour away, so more water can evaporate.

items.prompt: A cold glass of iced tea sits on a table. Soon, water drops form on the outside. Where do they come from?

options.why: Glass is waterproof. The drops come from the air.

options.text: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass.
The ice melts through the glass.
options.why: Ice cannot pass through glass.
Tables do not make water.

hints: The drops are on the outside of the glass.
Air contains invisible water vapour.
What happens to water vapour when it touches something cold?
items.explanation: The air has water vapour in it. When it touches the cold glass, it cools and condenses into drops of water.

items.prompt: Which change can be easily reversed?

options.why: You cannot unbake a cake. The change is permanent.
Burnt paper cannot turn back into paper.
A fried egg cannot become raw again.

hints: A reversible change can be undone.
Think about cooling something back down.
Which one can be cooled to get the same material back?
items.explanation: Melted chocolate becomes solid again when it cools, so melting is reversible. Baking, burning and frying make new materials.

items.prompt: The table shows melting points. The room is 45 °C. Choose 2 materials that will be melted.

head: Material
Melting point (°C)
figure.alt: Table of melting points: ice 0 °C, chocolate 35 °C, candle wax 60 °C, iron 1538 °C.

options.why: Candle wax needs 60 °C to melt. The room is cooler than that.
Iron needs over 1500 °C to melt.

hints: A material melts when it is hotter than its melting point.
Compare each melting point with 45 °C.
Which melting points are lower than the room temperature?
items.explanation: Ice melts at 0 °C and chocolate at 35 °C, so both are melted at 45 °C. Wax needs 60 °C and iron needs much more.

items.prompt: The same amount of water is put in a wide plate and a narrow cup. Both sit in the sun. Which loses water faster?

options.text: the cup, because it is taller
options.why: Being taller does not help water evaporate.

options.text: both the same, because they hold the same amount
options.why: The amount is the same, but the surface is different.

options.text: neither, because water only evaporates when it boils
options.why: Water evaporates at any temperature, just faster when warm.

options.text: the plate, because more of the water's surface touches the air

hints: Water evaporates from its surface.
Which container spreads the water out more?
Compare the size of the water's surface in each.
items.explanation: Water evaporates from its surface. The plate spreads the water out, so more surface touches the air and it evaporates faster.

items.prompt: When water vapour cools and turns back into a liquid, it ___.
hints: Think about a cold mirror in a steamy bathroom.
This is the opposite of evaporating.
The word starts with con.
items.explanation: Water vapour condenses when it cools, turning back into liquid water.

items.prompt: Which tool do we use to measure temperature?

options.why: A ruler measures length.
A jug measures how much liquid there is.
A stopwatch measures time.

hints: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is.
The tool has a scale marked in degrees.
It has a bulb and a thin tube.
items.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius.

items.prompt: Tom puts a thermometer into a cup of warm water. What temperature does it show?

figure.alt: A thermometer from 0 to 100 °C, marked every 10 degrees. The liquid stops at the 70 °C line.

hints: Look at where the liquid stops.
Find the nearest numbered line.
Read the number on that line.
items.explanation: The liquid stops at the line for 70 degrees Celsius.

items.prompt: The water was 90 °C and then cooled to the temperature shown. By how many degrees did it cool?

figure.alt: A thermometer from 0 to 100 °C, marked every 5 degrees. The liquid stops at the 35 °C line.

hints: First read the thermometer.
Subtract the new reading from 90.
The marks go up in 5s.
items.explanation: The thermometer reads 35 °C. The water cooled by 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.

items.prompt: Tap the place where most water evaporates.

figure.alt: A scene with a sun at top left, a cloud at top right, a mountain at right and blue sea along the bottom.

hints: Evaporation turns liquid water into a gas.
It needs a big area of liquid water and some warmth.
Look for the largest area of water.
items.explanation: The sea is a large body of liquid water warmed by the sun, so a lot of water evaporates from it.

items.prompt: Label the water cycle. One label does not belong.

figure.alt: A water cycle picture. A sun is at top left, a large cloud at top right, and blue sea along the bottom. An arrow rises from the sea on the left. A water drop falls from the cloud towards the sea on the right.

hints: The arrow shows liquid water becoming a gas.
In the cloud, water vapour cools and becomes drops.
The falling drops are rain.
items.explanation: Water evaporates from the sea, condenses to make a cloud, and falls as rain (precipitation).

items.prompt: Dewi leaves 30 ml of water in three saucers for 2 days. Fill in the water lost.
items.caption: Water in saucers
head: Place
Start (ml)
After 2 days (ml)
Water lost (ml)
hints: Water lost is the start amount minus the amount left.
For the shady shelf, work out 30 - 18.
For the fridge, work out 30 - 24.
items.explanation: The shelf lost 30 - 18 = 12 ml and the fridge lost 30 - 24 = 6 ml.

items.prompt: Look at Dewi's table. Which conclusion does it support?

head: Place
Start (ml)
After 2 days (ml)
Water lost (ml)
figure.alt: Table of water in three saucers. Sunny windowsill: 30 ml at the start, 5 ml after 2 days, 25 ml lost. Shady shelf: 30, 18, 12 lost. Fridge: 30, 24, 6 lost.

options.text: Water evaporates faster in a colder place
options.why: The fridge is the coldest place and lost the least water.
The saucer in the fridge still lost 6 ml.

options.text: Water evaporates faster in a warmer place
Water does not evaporate in a fridge
options.why: The fridge saucer lost 6 ml, so some water still evaporated.

hints: Find the place that lost the most water.
Find the place that lost the least.
Compare the temperatures of those two places.
items.explanation: The warm sunny windowsill lost the most water and the cold fridge lost the least. Warmer places make evaporation faster.

items.prompt: Amara tests if a fan makes wet cloths dry faster. Choose 2 things to keep the same.

options.why: This is the one thing she changes on purpose.

options.text: the amount of water in each cloth
how long it takes the cloth to dry
options.why: This is what she measures, so it is expected to differ.

hints: She changes only the fan.
Everything else must be the same to be fair.
Pick the two things that are neither changed nor measured.
items.explanation: Only the fan changes. The size of the cloths and the amount of water must be the same so the test is fair.

items.prompt: Put the water cycle in order, starting at the sea.
items: The sun warms the sea water
The vapour cools and condenses into cloud
Rain falls back into the sea
hints: The sun warms the sea first.
Water vapour must cool before it makes cloud.
The last step is the water returning to the sea.
items.explanation: The sun warms the sea so water evaporates. The vapour cools and condenses into a cloud, and then falls as rain.

items.prompt: Match each event to the change of state.
pairs: an ice lolly drips in the sun
mist forms on a cold mirror
water in a freezer turns hard
hints: Think about which way the water is changing.
Ice becomes water when heated.
Water vapour becomes water when cooled.
items.explanation: A dripping ice lolly is melting. Hair drying is evaporation. Mist on a cold mirror is condensation. Water becoming ice is freezing.

items.prompt: Putri boils a pan of water until it is dry. Where did the water go?

options.why: Water does not disappear. It changes state.
A metal pan cannot soak up water.
Heating changes water to a gas, not a solid.

options.text: Into the air as invisible water vapour

hints: Heating turns liquid water into a gas.
The gas is called water vapour.
Water vapour mixes with the air.
items.explanation: The heat turned the liquid water into water vapour, which mixed with the air in the room.

items.prompt: Chocolate melts at 30 °C. It melts in the hand of Kofi (34 °C) but not in his bag (25 °C). Why?

options.text: His hand makes chocolate melt by touching it
options.why: Touch alone does nothing. The heat from the hand matters.

options.text: His hand is warmer than the melting point and the bag is cooler
Chocolate melts only when it is in a bag
options.why: The bag was cooler than 30 °C, so it did not melt there.

options.text: The bag is made of cold material
options.why: The bag is just as cool as the air around it, 25 °C.

hints: A solid melts when it is hotter than its melting point.
Compare 34 °C and 25 °C with 30 °C.
One is above the melting point and one is below.
items.explanation: The hand at 34 °C is above the melting point of 30 °C, so the chocolate melts. The bag at 25 °C is below it.

items.prompt: When a liquid cools down and becomes a solid, it ___.
hints: Water does this in a freezer.
The word ends with -s.
The word starts with the letter f.
items.explanation: A liquid that cools to become a solid freezes.

items.prompt: When ice melts it changes from a ___ to a ___.
hints: Ice is hard.
Melted ice can be poured.
Think about the order of the changes.
items.explanation: Ice is a solid. When it melts it becomes liquid water.

items.prompt: The chart shows how long an ice cube takes to melt at different room temperatures. Predict the time at 25 °C.

figure.alt: Bar chart of minutes for an ice cube to melt. At 10 °C: 40. At 20 °C: 25. At 30 °C: 15. At 40 °C: 8.

options.why: That is the time at 40 °C, which is much warmer.
That is too short. It is shorter than the time at 30 °C, but 25 °C is cooler than 30 °C.
This is nearly as long as at 10 °C. 25 °C is much warmer than that.

hints: Find the bars for 20 °C and 30 °C.
The answer is between those two times.
The warmer the room, the shorter the time.
items.explanation: 25 °C is halfway between 20 °C (25 minutes) and 30 °C (15 minutes). So the time is about 20 minutes.

items.prompt: Yuki simmers a pan of water for 20 minutes. It loses 100 ml. She repeats it with a lid on. What happens?

options.text: It loses more water because the lid traps heat
options.why: The lid does not remove water. The vapour is caught and returns.

options.text: It loses the same amount because the lid is irrelevant
options.why: The lid stops vapour escaping, so less water is lost.

options.text: It loses less water because vapour condenses on the lid and drips back
It loses no water at all because the lid seals the pan
options.why: A little vapour still escapes, so some water is still lost.

hints: Water vapour rises from the hot pan.
The lid is cooler than the vapour.
Think about what vapour does when it touches something cold.
items.explanation: The vapour hits the cooler lid, condenses to liquid and drips back. Less vapour escapes, so less water is lost.

items.prompt: Sort each event by whether heat is added or taken away.

items.text: mist forming on a cold window
butter getting hard in a fridge

hints: Melting and evaporation need heat.
Freezing and condensation need cooling.
Think about whether the thing gets warmer or cooler.
items.explanation: Chocolate melting, a puddle drying and wax melting need heat. Ice forming, mist on a cold window and butter hardening need heat to be taken away.
